old: "What a fool I am, getting involved," he thought with a sudden feeling of oppressive annoyance. "What idiocy!" In his vexation he picked up the candle, intending to find the ragged attendant and leave at once. "Damn the child!" he thought, reaching for the door — but he turned back to check whether she was sleeping. He carefully lifted the blanket. The child was sleeping soundly and had gotten warm. Her pale cheeks had flushed. But the flush seemed brighter and coarser than a normal rosy glow of childhood. "It's a fever flush," Svidrigailov thought. It looked more like the flush from alcohol — as though she'd been given a full glass of wine. Her crimson lips were hot and burning. But what was this? He suddenly thought her long dark lashes were quivering, as though the lids were lifting and a sly, crafty eye was peeping out with an unchildlike wink — as if the little girl weren't asleep at all but pretending. Yes — that was it. Her lips parted in a smile. The corners of her mouth quivered, as though she were trying to hold it back. But now she gave up all pretense. It was a grin — a broad grin. There was something shameless, provocative in that utterly unchildlike face; it was corruption, the face of a prostitute, the brazen face of a French harlot. Now both eyes were open wide, turning a glowing, shameless stare on him; they laughed, they invited... There was something infinitely hideous and revolting in that laugh, in those eyes, in such depravity in the face of a child. "What? At five years old?" Svidrigailov whispered in genuine horror. "What does this mean?" And now she turned to him, her little face all aglow, reaching out her arms... "Accursed child!" Svidrigailov cried, raising his hand to strike her — but at that moment he woke up.

old: A thick, milky fog lay over the city. Svidrigailov walked along the slippery, dirty wooden pavement toward the Little Neva. He was picturing the waters of the Little Neva, swollen in the night — Petrovsky Island, the wet paths, the wet grass, the wet trees and bushes — and finally, that bush... He began irritably staring at the buildings, trying to think of something else. Not a cab or a soul in the street. The bright yellow little wooden houses looked dirty and dejected with their shutters closed. The cold and damp penetrated his whole body, and he started shivering. Now and then he passed a shop sign and read each one carefully. At last he reached the end of the wooden pavement and came to a large stone building. A dirty, shivering dog crossed his path, tail between its legs. A man in a greatcoat lay face down across the sidewalk, dead drunk. He glanced at him and walked on. A tall tower loomed on his left. The baseline narrows the general 'a human being' to 'she' (the old woman) and adds the hedge 'at least', which reshapes his reasoning.

old: a loud, persistent hammering — someone seemed to be hammering...
new: a loud, persistent knocking — someone seemed to be hammering...
reason: The restored clause repeats 'hammering' twice in one sentence. The source has 'a loud continuous knocking; someone seemed to be hammering...'.

old: "No, of course not. Here, take this one
new: "No, of course you don't. Here, take this one
reason: Sonia answers for him, but "No, of course not" sounds like Raskolnikov's reply; the attribution comes only at the end of the paragraph, so a listener assigns the speech to the wrong person.

old: nearly half a liter of blood
new: nearly a pint of blood
reason: A metric 'liter' in a Petersburg official's speech of the 1860s jars with the period world. [verifier-modified: The anachronism is real, but 'tumblerful' is not in the source either. The source (Garnett) says 'nearly a pint of blood'.]

old: At last she asked to be raised up.
new: At last Katerina Ivanovna asked to be raised up.
reason: The preceding sentence ends on Sonia, so 'she' reads as Sonia though it is the dying Katerina Ivanovna who asks.

old: She looked at her with suffering.
new: She looked at Sonia with a face of suffering.
reason: Two bare pronouns for two women in one short sentence; naming Sonia makes the look clear to a listener. [verifier-modified: Naming Sonia is right: Katerina looks at Sonia. The source says 'with a face of suffering', and bare 'with suffering' is awkward, so the source phrase is restored.]

old: he thought he would have run away from her.
new: he thought he would run away from her.
reason: The certainty repair restored 'he thought', but 'would have run' after the present-tense condition 'if she kept staring' is a tense clash. 'Would run' keeps the hedge and matches 'kept'.

old: it must be for some kind of strongbox, and that perhaps everything was hidden there
new: it must be for some kind of strongbox, and perhaps everything was hidden there
reason: The certainty repair ('and that perhaps everything was hidden there') restored the source's 'perhaps' but left a dangling 'that' after the dash-interrupted clause. Dropping 'that' keeps the hedge. Folds in accessibility item 0.

old: He said a couple of words in French with a foreigner
new: He said a couple of words in French to a foreigner
reason: The invention repair removed 'even exchanged' but kept its preposition: 'said ... with a foreigner' is unidiomatic. The source has 'said a couple of words in French to a foreigner'.

old: at billiards, at Gambrinus's.
new: at billiards, at Gambrinus's tavern.
reason: A listener cannot tell that Gambrinus's is a tavern; one word locates it.

old: That's weird.
new: That's odd.
reason: Casual modern 'weird' jars in an 1860s voice; 'odd' does the same job.

old: "That fellow's had quite a workout!"
new: "That fellow's been on a spree!"
reason: 'Workout' is a twentieth-century gym word that breaks the period world. [verifier-modified: The source has 'My word, he has been going it!', which is slang for drinking or living fast: the sweat-soaked man is taken for a drunk. 'Workout' is anachronistic, but 'hard at it' suggests he has been working. 'On a spree' keeps the drunkenness.]

old: people of every sort and both genders
new: people of every sort and both sexes
reason: 'Both genders' is modern usage; 'both sexes' is the period phrase.

old: with zero interest
new: without the slightest interest
reason: 'Zero interest' is modern slang.

old: and his honor arrived drunk
new: and the gentleman arrived drunk
reason: Heard aloud next to 'Mr. Captain', 'his honor' sounds like the officer, not the drunken writer.

old: his sentimental outburst to Ilya Petrovitch
new: his sentimental outburst in front of Ilya Petrovitch
reason: He addressed Nikodim Fomitch, not Ilya Petrovitch, so 'to' misstates who he spoke to.

old: but withdrew the moment he came to
new: but withdrew the moment Raskolnikov came to
reason: The two 'he's make it sound as if Ilya Petrovitch had fainted and come to.

old: even when he had decided in the night, without hesitation
new: even when he had decided in the night to throw it all in the water, without hesitation
reason: The listener is not told what he decided, so the sentence loses its object.

old: So I haven't come to Razumihin on purpose?
new: Why, I've come to Razumihin's without meaning to!
reason: The negative question reads backwards on first hearing; the thought is that he arrived without intending to. [verifier-modified: The source has 'why, I have not come to Razumihin of my own accord!'. That is an exclamation of discovery, and his doubt only follows it ('have I come on purpose or...'). The proposed question weakens the assertion, so keep the exclamation and the 'Why,'. The meaning 'without meaning to' is right.]

old: Rousseau was a kind of Radishchev.
new: Rousseau was a kind of Radishchev, our Russian radical.
reason: Radishchev is obscure to an English listener and the joke depends on knowing he was a radical writer.

old: so much so that it would be almost ill-bred in a man of society
new: so much so that it would be almost ill-bred for a man of society to go in for them
reason: 'it would be almost ill-bred' has no clear subject on first hearing; naming the action restores the logic. [verifier-modified: Real first-hearing gap (source is equally elliptical); 'to do it' is still vague. 'them' points back to the home-made sacred traditions, which is the source's sense.]

old: “It has acted violently,”
new: “It has hit her hard,”
reason: 'It has acted violently' is opaque out of context; the sense is that the news has struck her violently.

old: I have nothing else to fear either. Because you couldn't complain afterwards.
new: I have nothing else to fear either, because you couldn't complain afterwards.
reason: Detached 'Because' fragment reads as a slip; joining it keeps the reasoning in one breath.

old: cocked it, and laid it in her hand on the table
new: cocked it, and rested her hand holding it on the table
reason: 'laid it in her hand on the table' is a garbled image; she rests her hand with the revolver on the table.

old: only gradually working her way to Third Street
new: only gradually bringing the conversation round to Third Street
reason: 'working her way to Third Street' sounds like literal travel; the point is she circles back to homely local matters. [verifier-modified: Need is real ('working her way to' sounds like travel), but 'the everyday matters of' is an interpretation. Source: 'only by degrees brought the conversation round to Third Street'.]

old: he had recommended Raskolnikov to entrust her
new: he had advised Raskolnikov to entrust her
reason: 'recommended someone to do' is ungrammatical in modern English. [verifier-modified: Grammar fix is real, but 'urged' overstates the source's 'recommended'; 'advised' keeps the degree.]

old: with a copper Achilles helmet on his head
new: with a copper helmet like Achilles' on his head
reason: The watchman is then called 'Achilles' throughout; making the helmet comparison explicit tells the listener where the nickname comes from.

old: onetime fiancee
new: onetime fiancée
reason: Spelled 'fiancée' in the previous chapter; keep the spelling consistent.

old: He was beginning to feel for himself that
new: He himself was beginning to feel that
reason: Source: 'He began to feel himself that he was certainly forgetting things'. In modern English 'feel for himself' reads as 'pity himself'; 'He himself was beginning to feel' keeps the source sense.

old: all the pleasures of life are _nihil est_ -- nothing --
new: all the pleasures of life are nothing -- _nihil est_ --
reason: Source: 'all the attractions of life _nihil est_'. 'are _nihil est_' reads 'are is nothing'; putting the English first and the Latin as his flourish keeps the italic Latin and the gloss without the doubled verb.

old: (perhaps she saw that they were pretending) but she kept talking
new: (perhaps she saw that they were pretending), but she kept talking
reason: Source: '(she saw perhaps that they were pretending), but she still went on talking'. The comma before 'but' was lost when the dashes became parentheses.

old: what was good; could not decide whom to blame
new: what was good; they could not decide whom to blame
reason: The restored clause put a semicolon before a subjectless 'could not decide'. Source: 'they did not know whom to blame, whom to justify'.

old: turned off his path, and walked along it toward the Hay Market
new: turned off his path, and crossed the bridge toward the Hay Market
reason: 'walked along it' leaves unclear whether 'it' is the bridge or the path and what he actually did; 'crossed it' makes the route clear. [verifier-modified: Source: 'on reaching the bridge he stopped and turning out of his way along it went to the Hay Market'. The 'it' is the bridge. 'crossed it' would still leave 'it' pointing at 'his path', so name the bridge.]

old: The translator's note read:
new: Translator's note:
reason: A translator's footnote appears mid-scene as if it were narrative, and 'The translator's note read' sounds like an object in the story; it at least needs to be marked clearly as an editorial note (an editor may prefer to move it out of the reading text).

old: whom he had supported almost since he was thirteen
new: whom the student had supported almost since he was thirteen
reason: With Raskolnikov and the student both in the sentence, 'he' is ambiguous about who supported the father from age thirteen.

old: their mother overhearing her talk in her sleep
new: their mother overhearing Dounia talk in her sleep
reason: 'her' could be the mother or Dounia; naming Dounia shows who talked in her sleep.

old: he smiled strangely at his sister and Razumihin's passionate plans
new: he smiled strangely at the passionate plans of his sister and Razumihin
reason: Heard aloud, 'smiled strangely at his sister' first sounds complete, so the listener has to reparse the sentence.

old: her old, worn burnous
new: her old, worn burnous cloak
reason: 'Burnous' is an obscure period garment; adding 'cloak' tells the listener what it is and keeps the word.

old: Whether I could step over the line or not. Whether I dared to stoop down and pick up power, or not. Whether I am
new: Whether I can step over the line or not. Whether I dare to stoop down and pick it up, or not. Whether I am
reason: Source: 'Whether I can step over barriers or not, whether I dare stoop to pick up or not, whether I am a trembling creature or whether I have the _right_'. 'power' is an invented object for 'pick up' (Garnett names none). The past 'could'/'dared' also clashes with the present 'am'/'have' that follow in the same series; the source uses present tense throughout.

old: I'd really come chiefly to show
new: I'd come chiefly to show
reason: Restored 'chiefly' (source: "I'd gone in chiefly to show") now sits beside the baseline's 'really', giving a redundant 'really ... chiefly'. Drop 'really'; the source has only 'chiefly'.

old: at eleven o'clock sharp the next morning he was surprised
new: at eleven o'clock sharp the next morning, he was surprised
reason: Removing ', as requested,' also removed the comma that closed the long 'When...' clause; restore it so the main clause is clear.

old: but that very uniqueness, her trace of education
new: but the very things that set her apart, her trace of education
reason: Right after 'not unique or even infrequent', 'that very uniqueness' sounds self-contradictory to a listener.

old: "I'll become one myself soon! It's contagious!"
new: "I'll become one myself soon! It's contagious!" he thought.
reason: The line has no speaker tag, so a listener cannot tell that it is Raskolnikov's private thought rather than something Sonia says aloud.

old: She's mad and consumptive
new: Katerina Ivanovna is mad and consumptive
reason: Coming right after 'if you're really taken to the hospital', 'She' could be heard as Sonia herself.

old: the old Austrian _Hofkriegsrath_
new: the old Austrian war council, the _Hofkriegsrath_
reason: The German term is opaque when heard, and 'war council' lets the Napoleon and General Mack joke land.

old: don't consider that 'when they overstep all obstacles,' as you put it so wittily yesterday.
new: don't take that into account when they 'overstep all obstacles,' as you put it so wittily yesterday.
reason: As written, the sentence breaks off: 'don't consider that' leads into a clause that is never finished, so it sounds ungrammatical.

old: No, I'm only wondering that you're too adaptable.
new: No, I'm only surprised that you're too adaptable a man.
reason: 'wondering that you're' is ungrammatical/archaic; source 'I am only wondering at your being too adaptable a man' means surprise, and the restored 'a man' was still missing.

old: or progress, maybe, perhaps
new: or even progress, maybe
reason: Source 'or progress, indeed, maybe' has one hedge; 'indeed' is an intensifier ('even'), not a second hedge. 'maybe, perhaps' doubles the uncertainty and reads as a stutter the source does not have.

old: instead of traveling
new: instead of the journey
reason: Source: 'Perhaps I'll get married instead of the journey.' 'The journey' is Svidrigaïlov's code word for suicide, echoed in 21.101, 21.121 and this paragraph's opening; 'traveling' breaks the motif.

old: a conceit that bordered on smug foolishness
new: a conceit carried to the point of smug foolishness
reason: 'smug foolishness' is a fair rendering of 'fatuity', but source says 'a conceit to the point of fatuity' (it reached it); 'bordered on' (kept from baseline) softens the narrator's judgement.

old: all sorts of schemes
new: all sorts of devices
reason: Source: 'by all sorts of devices'. 'schemes' adds an implication of dishonesty the source leaves open.

old: the Dussauts,
new: restaurants like Dussaut's,
reason: 'the Dussauts' sounds like a family; a listener cannot tell it is a fashionable restaurant. [verifier-modified: Need is real (reads as a family), but source 'Dussauts' is plural/generic; 'restaurants like Dussaut's' keeps that instead of naming one restaurant.]

old: thirty thousand silver
new: thirty thousand in silver
reason: 'thirty thousand silver' reads as a slip; 'in silver' is the natural currency idiom.

old: Aniska can't make like this.
new: Aniska can't make one like this.
reason: A missing word makes the ghost's line ungrammatical.

old: You say 'you or he,'
new: You say 'you or him,'
reason: Luzhin quotes Dounia, but she said 'it's either you or him', so the quote does not match.

old: just to avoid borrowing from that man until he offered help.
new: just to avoid borrowing from that man Luzhin until he offered help.
reason: Coming right after the talk about Svidrigaïlov, 'that man' is misleading (she means Luzhin), and 'until he offered help' is muddled. [verifier-modified: Ambiguity after the Svidrigaïlov talk is real, but 'that man' carries her disdain and 'himself' is not in Garnett; keep 'that man' and add the name.]

old: in German—that had been a ploy
new: in German. That had been a ploy
reason: Too many dashes in a row make the sentence lose its thread when heard aloud.

old: I'll pawn the watch tomorrow
new: I'll pawn your watch tomorrow
reason: 'the watch' is unanchored; it is Dounia's watch, mentioned earlier.

old: Oh, I'm quite obliged to...
new: Oh, I really have to...
reason: 'quite obliged' sounds like thanks rather than necessity, which misleads the listener.

old: vanished almost immediately
new: vanished immediately
reason: Source: 'vanished immediately'. 'almost' adds a hedge the source does not have.

old: she'd start with eager questions about Paris
new: she'd start with interested, almost eager questions about Paris
reason: Source: 'interested and almost eager questions'. Dropping 'almost' turns a hedged degree into a flat one.

old: On other occasions this had been quite impressive
new: On other occasions this had, of course, been very impressive
reason: Source: 'this had of course been very impressive'. The narrator's ironic 'of course' is dropped and 'very' is weakened to 'quite'.

old: One last request, if I may,
new: If anything happens, I have one request to make,
reason: Source: 'If anything happens, I have one request to make of you'. 'last' is invented and the conditional that opens Porfiry's circling approach ('If anything happens... If anything were to happen') is dropped.

old: Just as a man might endure half an hour of mortal terror with a robber — yet when the knife is finally at his throat, he feels no fear.
new: So a man will sometimes endure half an hour of mortal terror with a robber, yet when the knife is finally at his throat, he feels no fear.
reason: The sentence is a fragment ('Just as...' with no main clause), which is hard to follow when heard. [verifier-modified: The fragment is real. But the proposal invents 'alone' and still loses the source's 'sometimes'. Source: 'So a man will sometimes go through half an hour of mortal terror with a brigand, yet when the knife is at his throat at last, he feels no fear.']

old: There have been Wanderers in his family
new: There have been Wanderers — members of a religious sect — in his family
reason: A listener hears the translator's note only as a detached line afterwards; a short inline gloss tells them who the Wanderers are at the moment it matters.

old: because I'm such a Schiller?
new: because I'm such a Schiller, such an idealist?
reason: This is the first use of 'Schiller' as shorthand for a romantic idealist, and a listener will not know the allusion. [verifier-modified: A gloss helps, but 'starry-eyed' adds a colouring of the translator's own. The source itself pairs the two words at 34.75 ('You--a Schiller, you--an idealist!'), so reuse that. Also, this is not the first Schiller reference, since 'Schilleresque' appears in Part 1.]

old: in this one is bound to go to excess
new: in this, one is bound to go to excess
reason: Without the comma, 'this one' is misread as a noun phrase.

old: She thought it showed I was unwilling to deceive her by warning her in advance
new: She thought that by warning her in advance I showed I was unwilling to deceive her
reason: The misplaced 'by warning her in advance' makes the sentence hard to follow on first hearing.

old: _la nature et la vérité_! Ha-ha!
new: _la nature et la vérité_ — nature and truth! Ha-ha!
reason: This French phrase is left unglossed, while the others nearby are glossed.

old: _O la vertu
new: _Où la vertu
reason: The Molière line is 'Où la vertu va-t-elle se nicher?'; 'O' is a misspelling.

old: Raskolnikov remembered and thought of it, but did not ask.
new: Raskolnikov thought of that as he looked at it, but did not ask.
reason: Source: 'Raskolnikov thought of that looking at it, but he did not ask.' 'looking at it' was dropped, and 'remembered and thought of it' says the same thing twice.

old: before the day of the confession.
new: before the fatal day of the confession.
reason: Source: 'before the fatal day of the confession'. 'fatal' was dropped.

old: about her hopes for his future. Her fantasies
new: about her hopes for his future... Her fantasies
reason: Source: 'of her hopes of his future.... Her fancies'. The mother's talk trails off in the source. Restore the ellipsis in the chapter's '...' style.

old:
soldier,
Don't
new: soldier, Don't
reason: The source runs the song fragment on one line ('Oh, my handsome soldier Don't beat me for nothing,'); this is the only literal line break in the whole edition and renders inconsistently. Replace it with a space; the comma is kept as a readable pause.

old: God, the idiotic ideas that come into one's head.
new: What idiotic ideas come into one's head.
reason: Source: 'What idiotic ideas come into one's head.' The exclamation 'God,' is not in the source (inherited from the baseline); it adds an invocation that the source does not have, so religious language gets invented. The contraction edits in this paragraph are otherwise correct.

old: He had gone terribly pale
new: Raskolnikov had gone terribly pale
reason: The preceding sentence has Zametov as subject, so 'He had gone pale' first reads as Zametov; naming Raskolnikov fixes it for a listener.

old: "Shut up and the door freshly painted.
new: "Closed up, and the door freshly painted.
reason: Heard aloud, 'Shut up' sounds like a rude command rather than 'closed and locked'. [verifier-modified: The need is real because 'Shut up' heard aloud sounds like a command. But source 'It's shut up' means closed, not necessarily locked; 'Closed up' is faithful.]

old: "Is the assistant there?"
new: "Is the assistant superintendent there?"
reason: 'The assistant' alone leaves a listener unsure who is meant; the police rank points to the officer Raskolnikov is thinking of.

old: He stumbled forward
new: Raskolnikov stumbled forward
reason: Right after 'he flung him', the next 'He' reads as the manager; naming Raskolnikov makes it clear.

old: a kammerjunker just arrived
new: a kammerjunker -- a gentleman of the court -- just arrived
reason: 'Kammerjunker' is an obscure court title; a brief gloss keeps Katerina Ivanovna's boast intelligible.

old: The prince knew me as a girl
new: The prince -- the Governor-General -- knew me as a girl
reason: No prince has been mentioned, so a listener cannot tell that 'the prince' is the Governor-General just named.

old: a kerchief from the chest over
new: a kerchief from the trunk over
reason: In a scene about a crushed chest, 'from the chest' is ambiguous aloud; 'trunk' names the piece of furniture.

old: She was at the bottom of the staircase, stopped one step above him.
new: She had reached the bottom of the staircase and stopped short one step above him.
reason: As written the sentence is garbled and self-contradictory: she can't be at the bottom and also a step above him. [verifier-modified: The need is real because the candidate's comma splice is garbled. But the proposal changes the subject to 'He', and the source's subject is 'She': 'She was at the bottom of the staircase and stopped short a step above him' (she had caught up with him at the foot of the stairs). Keep her as the subject and fix the syntax.]

old: had the highest opinion of his intelligence, and sometimes even gloated over his reflection in the mirror.
new: had the highest opinion of his intelligence and abilities, and sometimes, when alone, even gloated over his reflection in the mirror.
reason: Source: 'had the highest opinion of his intelligence and capacities, and sometimes even gloated in solitude over his image in the glass.' 'in solitude' (private self-admiration) and 'capacities' are dropped. This predates round F/AV but is inside the re-verified paragraph.

old: you must refuse Luzhin. so that
new: you must refuse Luzhin, so that
reason: The F repair restoring 'so that we may never hear his name again' left a full stop before the lowercase purpose clause, breaking the sentence. Source: 'you must refuse Luzhin, so that we may never hear his name again.' (Folds accessibility item 0.)

old: the three fish that support the world
new: the three fish that hold up the world in the old tales
reason: The folk-cosmology image of three fish holding up the earth is obscure to a listener; a short cue unlocks it.

old: I write in the expectation that Rodion Romanovitch, who seemed so ill during my visit, had suddenly recovered two hours later
new: I write on the assumption that Rodion Romanovitch, who seemed so ill during my visit, suddenly recovered two hours later
reason: 'Expectation that ... had recovered' is tense-tangled; 'belief' also sets up the letter's next line, 'I was confirmed in this belief'. [verifier-modified: The tense tangle is real, but the source reads 'I write on the assumption that Rodion Romanovitch who appeared so ill at my visit, suddenly recovered two hours later'. 'Assumption' keeps Luzhin's wording; the next line's 'confirmed in that belief' still follows naturally.]

old: "The queen who darned stockings in prison,"
new: "Marie Antoinette, the queen who darned stockings in prison,"
reason: The unnamed allusion is hard to place by ear; naming the queen unlocks it.

old: Among dozens—perhaps hundreds of thousands—you'd hardly find one.
new: Among tens of thousands—perhaps hundreds of thousands—you'd hardly find one.
reason: 'Among dozens' heard on its own suggests a few dozen people, which garbles the doctor's point.

old: "Ach!" Razumihin was exclaiming
new: "A-ach!" Razumihin was exclaiming
reason: The fix replaced baseline 'Ha!' with 'Ach!', but the source has the drawn-out 'A-ach!' (Razumihin is cut off mid-exclamation by the door opening). Keep the source's elongation.

old: he isn't cunning, not experienced
new: he is not cunning, not experienced
reason: Contraction pass: source 'he is not cunning, not practised' is an emphatic parallel of negations in Razumihin's pronouncement ('I maintain'). 'isn't cunning, not experienced' breaks the parallel and weakens the stress; keep the long form here.

old: I wanted to blow him up too
new: I wanted to give him a piece of my mind too
reason: "Blow him up" is heard as "explode him"; the meaning is to scold him.

old: in the empty apartment while Nikolay and Dmitri had just run out
new: in the empty apartment, which Nikolay and Dmitri had just run out of
reason: "While ... had just run out" is tense-tangled and hard to parse on first hearing.

old: Razumihin continued, whose easy familiarity seemed
new: Razumihin continued. His easy familiarity seemed
reason: The relative clause "whose" hangs off the verb instead of a noun, which is ungrammatical.

old: His dark mutton-chop whiskers framed both sides nicely, growing thick on his shining, clean-shaven chin.
new: His dark mutton-chop whiskers framed his face nicely on both sides, growing thick down around his shining, clean-shaven chin.
reason: Whiskers "growing thick on" a "clean-shaven chin" sounds self-contradictory. [verifier-modified: The need is real, but the proposal moves the thick growth to the cheeks. Source: whiskers 'made an agreeable setting on both sides, growing thickly upon his shining, clean-shaven chin' (i.e. thickening toward/around the chin). Keep the thickening at the chin while removing the contradiction.]

old: how sick, how sick I was of going over it all!
new: how sick, how sick I was then of going over it all!
reason: Source: 'And how sick, how sick I was then of going over it all!' The candidate drops 'then', so the weariness is no longer placed in the period before the murder. Restoring it costs one word.

old: I clearly sensed that I wasn't Napoleon.
new: I clearly sensed, of course, that I wasn't Napoleon.
reason: Source: 'I felt clearly of course that I wasn't Napoleon.' The candidate drops 'of course', which marks the conclusion as self-evident (a certainty marker).

old: I needed to find out, and find out quickly,
new: I needed to find out then, and find out quickly,
reason: Source: 'I wanted to find out then and quickly whether I was a louse'. The candidate keeps 'quickly' but drops 'then', which carries the urgency of that moment.

old: in a phalanstery, one of their socialist communes!
new: in a phalanstery, one of their socialist communal houses!
reason: The gloss is broadly right but imprecise: a phalanstery is Fourier's communal building that houses a socialist community, not the community itself. The sentence is about walls, rooms and corridors, so the building sense is the accurate one.

old: almost correctly—perhaps perfectly so.
new: almost correctly—perhaps, if you like, perfectly so.
reason: Source "perhaps, if you like, perfectly so": the hedge 'if you like' is dropped, so he concedes more firmly than the source.

old: Napoleon, and so on—were without exception
new: Napoleon, and so on, were without exception
reason: The fidelity edit replaced 'men—Lycurgus' with 'men, such as Lycurgus' but left the closing dash, which now has no opening partner.

old: might at last produce one person in a thousand
new: might at last produce perhaps one person in a thousand
reason: Source "to bring into the world at last perhaps one man out of a thousand": his 'perhaps' is dropped, which makes his figure more certain than the source. This passage is his 'roughly, approximately' theory.

old: I don't think there was any apartment open. No,
new: I don't think there was a flat open anywhere. No,
reason: The same paragraph now says 'a flat like that open'; the source says 'a flat open anywhere' both times. Mixing 'flat' and 'apartment' within one answer is the defect the reviewer fixed at 19.62, and 'anywhere' is part of his over-insistence.

old: "At last he sees through Zametov!"
new: "At last he sees through him!"
reason: Source "At last he sees through him!" leaves the referent open, and the Russian ('At last he's guessed!') names no one. Naming Zametov adds an interpretation. Directly after 'As for Zametov—', 'him' is already clear to a listener.

old: waiting for 'universal happiness.'
new: waiting for the 'happiness of all.'
reason: The source repeats the quoted slogan 'the happiness of all' four times in this monologue. Varying it to 'universal happiness' breaks the obsessive repetition of a phrase he is quoting.

old: "What a simple-hearted fool he is!"
new: "What a simple-hearted fool he is!" Raskolnikov thought.
reason: Unattributed inner thought directly after Razumihin's line; a listener may hear it as Razumihin speaking or as Raskolnikov saying it aloud.

old: "Listen to that! How that idea
new: "Listen to that!" he thought. "How that idea
reason: This is Raskolnikov's private thought (Razumihin must not hear it), but nothing marks it as unspoken until the next paragraph.

old: likes to put people on, or rather
new: likes to fool people, or rather
reason: 'Put people on' is modern American slang and may be unclear; 'fool' keeps the meaning in period register.

old: "The most important thing: does Porfiry know
new: "The most important thing," he thought, "does Porfiry know
reason: Follows Razumihin's spoken line with no attribution, so a listener hears Razumihin asking whether Porfiry knows about the flat.
